title: Opening a Turkish bank account as a foreigner
excerpt: You can open a Turkish bank account as a foreigner, but the required documents depend on whether you’re a resident or a visitor. Residents usually open with their residence permit and Foreigner Identification Number (YKN); some banks also take non-residents with a passport, a tax number and proof of address. Requirements differ by bank and branch, so check the bank's own list and, if you're refused, ask what was missing.
bodyHtml:
A Turkish bank account is the key to everyday life in Türkiye—paying rent, shopping online, setting up automatic bill payments, and managing your finances locally. While you can get by without one initially, you’ll quickly find it essential.

What you need

  • Passport (original; copies aren’t enough).

  • A Turkish ID number — your Foreigner Identification Number (YKN) or a tax number. If you have a residence permit, you already have a YKN (it's on the card), and banks generally use that. If you don't, you'll need a tax number (Vergi Kimlik Numarası) — free, from a tax office or online (our tax number guide walks you through it). Which one a bank asks for depends on the bank and your status: İş Bankası, for example, accepts either; Kuveyt Türk asks residents for the YKN and non-residents for a tax-number document.

  • Proof of address — requirements vary by bank. Accepted documents may include:

    • A residence permit showing your registered address.

    • A recent Turkish utility bill.

    • An official address registration document.

    • In some cases, a notarised rental contract.

  • Turkish mobile phone number — required for SMS verification and mobile banking.

  • Residence permit — if you have one, bring it. Whether it's required depends on the bank, your residence status and the bank's customer checks: İş Bankası's published list, for example, asks for a valid passport or, where applicable, a residence permit. Having one generally makes things easier.

Which banks open accounts for foreigners

This article used to rank banks — which were "easiest" for non-residents, which "usually require" a residence permit. That ranking is gone, because it was the kind of claim that is confidently wrong at a counter on a given morning. Bank policy on foreign customers changes without notice, differs for resident and non-resident applicants, and is applied with real discretion at branch level. Kuveyt Türk, for one, publishes separate requirement sets for resident and non-resident foreign nationals — so even "this bank takes non-residents" is too coarse to act on.

Read the bank's own current requirements before you go, and take them with you:

  • Ziraat Bankası — ziraatbank.com.tr

  • Kuveyt Türk — kuveytturk.com.tr (separate pages for resident and non-resident foreign nationals)

  • Garanti BBVA — garantibbva.com.tr

  • İş Bankası — isbank.com.tr

  • Akbank — akbank.com

  • Yapı Kredi — yapikredi.com.tr

  • Enpara Bank — enpara.com, digital-only; separate from QNB Türkiye since August 2025, still part of QNB Group. Not for newcomers: its FAQ says foreign customers must have lived in Türkiye for at least six months, be resident here, have a YKN and speak Turkish.

In practice, two branches of the same bank can give you different answers with the same documents. But a refusal isn't always one branch's preference: banks are legally required to refuse an account when they can't complete the identity checks they must do, and some refusals are about eligibility. So ask what requirement wasn't met. If it's something you can fix, fix it; if the branch simply won't do it, another branch or bank may — but no branch can waive a legal requirement.

What tends to help:

  • Pick a branch in a neighbourhood with lots of foreign residents. Staff there have usually done this many times and have a routine; a branch in a quiet residential area may rarely onboard a foreigner.

  • Go early on a weekday. Account opening is slow, and a branch that is swamped at lunchtime is more likely to send you away.

  • Ask other members which branches are opening accounts for foreigners smoothly right now. That changes over time, and it is local knowledge you can't look up.

What to ask for when opening your account

  • Mobile banking activation — make sure your Turkish phone number is registered before leaving the branch. Most major banks' apps can run in English; set that up while someone is there to help.

  • Debit card (banka kartı) — many branches issue it immediately, while others mail it to your address within a few days.

  • TRY current account with IBAN — this is the account you’ll use for salary payments, rent, and receiving transfers from services like Wise.

  • USD and EUR accounts — useful if you receive or keep money in foreign currencies. Ask for these specifically, as they may not be opened automatically.

  • The fees — on foreign-currency accounts and on incoming international transfers. If money arrives from abroad regularly, this is the question that saves you the most.

Tip: Get your Turkish SIM first

Almost every bank uses SMS verification to activate online and mobile banking. Having an active Turkish SIM card before your appointment will make the process much smoother and can save you an extra trip. The order that works: SIM, then tax number, then bank — see our SIM card guide.

About foreign currency accounts

Most Turkish banks allow you to open USD and EUR accounts alongside your Turkish Lira account. However, bank exchange rates are often less competitive than specialist money transfer services.

For larger transfers — apartment deposits, tuition fees, moving savings into Türkiye — a money transfer service that pays Turkish lira straight into your Turkish bank account is often cheaper than letting the bank convert. Wise can still do that. What it can't do for customers registered in Türkiye is hold money: Wise says Türkiye-based customers can't receive money into a Wise account or convert between balances, so don't plan on a Wise balance as your local account. Rates and fees vary enough between banks and providers that it's worth comparing the final amount that actually arrives before you settle on one route for regular transfers.

Havale, EFT and FAST: know the difference before you pay rent

Paying by bank transfer is completely normal here — rent, a repair, splitting dinner. Turkish banking has three kinds of transfer, and the apps ask you to pick:

  • Havale — a transfer between two accounts at the same bank. Generally immediate; whether it costs anything depends on your bank, the channel and your account package — some banks charge even for app transfers.

  • EFT — a transfer to an account at a different bank, settled through the interbank system. It may carry a small fee depending on your account package. EFT is not the instant rail, and it does not run around the clock.

  • FAST — the Central Bank's instant payment system, and a separate thing from EFT. It moves money between banks 24/7, nights, weekends and public holidays included, settling in seconds, up to a per-transaction limit set by the Central Bank (currently ₺100,000, and revised from time to time). Most banking apps offer it as its own option; when the amount fits under the limit, this is usually the one you want.

You do not have to memorise which is which — enter the IBAN and the app works it out. It is worth knowing the words, though, because that is how the fee is described to you, and it explains why some landlords ask which bank you are with.

Money arriving from abroad

Incoming international transfers work fine, but they can be slower than a domestic transfer and are sometimes held while the bank asks where the money came from. A document request is usually routine compliance, and it catches people off guard when a deposit or a few months of savings lands.

Be ready: have a plain explanation and, for larger amounts, something documenting the source — a payslip, a sale contract, a transfer receipt from the sending bank. Review times vary, and only the bank can tell you when the money will be released, so don't plan a deadline (a rent deposit, a purchase) around money that is still in transit.
